A.explanation: This is $4/3 P \approx 1.3P$, which treats power as proportional to amplitude rather than to $\text{amplitude}^2$.

B.explanation: Intensity is $16$ times larger because $(4X)^2 = 16X^2$, and power is intensity times area $A/3$, giving $16/3 P \approx 5.3P$.

C.explanation: This omits the reduced area $A/3$ correctly and does not follow $P = I \times \text{area}$ with $I$ proportional to $\text{amplitude}^2$.

D.explanation: This multiplies the $16$ times intensity by $3$ instead of by $1/3$, giving $16 \times 3P = 48P$.

hints: Notice the two separate changes: amplitude $X$ to $4X$ and area $A$ to $A/3$, with frequency unchanged.
Recall how wave intensity $I = P/A$ depends on amplitude for the same frequency: $I$ is proportional to $\text{amplitude}^2$.
First find the new intensity factor of $16$, then multiply by the new area $A/3$ to get the new power in terms of $P$.
walkthrough: Write intensity as power per unit area: $I = P/A$ for the first beam and $I_{new} = P_{new}/(A/3)$ for the second beam.
Use the wave rule for constant frequency: intensity is proportional to $\text{amplitude}^2$, so $I_{new}/I = (4X)^2/X^2 = 16$.
Convert back to power using the new area: $P_{new} = I_{new} \times (A/3) = (16P/A) \times (A/3)$.
Simplify to $P_{new} = 16P/3 \approx 5.3P$. This is option B.
